games.title: Lunar Lander (1969)
games.note: Written by high school student Jim Storer. David Ahl called it the most popular computer game of its time.

games.title: Moonlander
games.note: Made to show off DEC's GT40 terminal. Land near the hidden McDonald's and the astronaut walks over to order.

games.title: Lunar Lander
games.note: Atari's first vector-graphics game. Players could add coins mid-game to buy more fuel.

games.title: Asteroids
games.note: Early units shipped in Lunar Lander cabinets because both games used the same vector hardware.

games.title: Defender
games.note: Players juggled a joystick and five buttons, including smart bombs and hyperspace.

games.title: Robotron: 2084
games.dev: Eugene Jarvis & Larry DeMar (Vid Kidz / Williams)
games.note: Jarvis's injured right hand was in a cast early on, which helped push the design to two joysticks.

games.title: Smash TV
games.note: A twin-stick shooter framed as a violent future game show with prizes.

games.title: Resogun
games.note: A PlayStation 4 launch game whose levels wrap around a cylinder built from voxels.

games.title: Nex Machina
games.note: Defender and Robotron creator Eugene Jarvis worked on it as a creative consultant.

games.title: Joust
games.note: Knights ride flying ostriches, and the higher lance wins each collision.

games.title: Balloon Fight
games.note: Programmed by Satoru Iwata at HAL Laboratory, who later became Nintendo's president.

games.title: Killer Queen
games.note: A ten-player arcade game where two teams of five play as bees.

games.title: Missile Command
games.note: Designer Dave Theurer has said that making it gave him nightmares about nuclear war.

games.title: Atari Football
games.note: Popularized the trackball controller. It was the second highest-earning US arcade game of 1979.

games.title: Tempest
games.note: Theurer said the idea came from a nightmare of monsters crawling out of a hole in the ground.

games.title: Tempest 2000
games.note: Jeff Minter's officially licensed update, made for the Atari Jaguar.

games.title: Centipede
games.note: Co-designed by Dona Bailey, one of the few women programming arcade games at the time.

games.title: Scramble
games.note: An early side-scrolling shooter with separate stages and a fuel gauge you refill by bombing fuel tanks.

games.title: Xevious
games.note: Endo hid secret Special Flags in it because he was a fan of Rally-X.

games.title: Gradius
games.note: Began as Scramble 2. Its Moai head enemies nod to the Nazca lines in Xevious.

games.title: TwinBee
games.note: You change power-ups by shooting floating bells until they change color.

games.title: River Raid
games.note: Carol Shaw designed and programmed it. An algorithm builds a river that never ends.

games.title: Chopper Command
games.note: Your helicopter protects a convoy of trucks from enemy jets and helicopters.

games.title: Fantasy Zone
games.note: Your ship, Opa-Opa, spends coins from defeated enemies at shops to buy new weapons.

games.title: R-Type
games.note: Built around the Force, a detachable pod that blocks shots and can be launched at enemies.

games.title: Rally-X
games.note: Players drive a race car around a scrolling maze to collect flags while dodging pursuing cars.

games.title: Moon Patrol
games.note: A moon buggy jumps craters and shoots upward over layered scenery that scrolls at different speeds.

games.title: Front Line
games.note: Your soldier can climb into tanks and must bail out when the tank is hit.

games.title: Commando
games.note: A lone soldier, Super Joe, runs and guns up a vertically scrolling battlefield.

games.title: Ikari Warriors
games.note: Rotary joysticks let two players aim in eight directions while running.

links.took: The landing puzzle of managing thrust and fuel to touch down gently.
links.added: Real-time vector graphics, light-pen control and a McDonald's on the Moon.
